paragraphs.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is an endocrine and non-endocrine tumor syndrome caused by heterozygous inactivating germline mutations or genomic rearrangements of the MAX gene (Haider et al., 2025; Charoenngam et al., 2026). Pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma (PPGL) and pituitary adenoma are the cardinal features. Parathyroid adenomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are less common (Maggacis et al., 2026). Seabrook et al. (2021) linked germline MAX mutations to pheochromocytomas, ganglioneuromas, neuroblastomas and pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, and possibly to parathyroid adenomas, chondrosarcoma and lung adenocarcinoma. On this basis they suggested that MAX is a novel multiple endocrine neoplasia gene.

paragraphs.text: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) updated a previously reported family with predisposition to pheochromocytoma (PCC) across 3 generations. The female proband (III-1) developed a neuroblastoma of the broad ligament at 17 months of age. At age 22 years she developed a right PCC, a ganglioneuroma at the site of the original neuroblastoma and an ileal schwannoma. Six years later she developed a left PCC with a mature ganglioneuroma. She went on to develop a metastatic leiomyosarcoma of the mesosigmoid, a hepatic carcinoma at age 42 and a uterine leiomyoma. Her paternal grandfather had bilateral PCC at age 70. Her youngest brother (III-3) presented at age 31 with a cardiomyopathy complicated by Takotsubo syndrome, which led to the diagnosis of bilateral PCC. His urinary normetanephrines were 8 times the upper limit while total metanephrines were normal, a pattern the authors noted is reminiscent of MAX-related tumors. At age 56 the paternal uncle (II-3) developed an 11-mm hypervascular right adrenal nodule with strong [18F]-DOPA uptake, which the authors considered suggestive of PCC or an adrenomedullary nodule.

paragraphs.text: Lian et al. (2024) described 3 Chinese probands. The first (family A) was a man diagnosed with right pheochromocytoma at age 24 years after more than 2 years of hypertension (200/110 mm Hg). At age 36 he developed a 3.8-cm left adrenal pheochromocytoma with elevated plasma norepinephrine, making his disease metachronous and bilateral. No pituitary abnormality or other neuroendocrine tumor was found. The second (family B) was a 34-year-old man with asymptomatic simultaneous bilateral adrenal masses (2.8 and 2.2 cm), normal blood pressure, and normal plasma catecholamines and metanephrines. Bilateral pheochromocytoma was confirmed after adrenal-sparing surgery. His pituitary and neck studies were normal, as were calcium, calcitonin, PTH, GH and prolactin. The third (family C) was a 64-year-old woman with occasional paroxysmal headache, elevated plasma norepinephrine and a 1.9-cm right pheochromocytoma.

paragraphs.text: In the same report, Lian et al. (2024) reviewed the literature on 109 MAX germline mutation carriers from 87 families. Of these, 101 (92.7%) developed pheochromocytoma at a mean age of 32.8 years (range, 13-80), with a male-to-female ratio of 1.3:1. The pheochromocytomas were bilateral in 59 (58.4%; 47 simultaneous, 12 metachronous) and metastatic in 19 (18.8%). Eleven (10.9%) also had thoracic or abdominal paraganglioma, and 1 had an isolated head and neck paraganglioma. Catecholamines were elevated in 61 of 63 carriers tested, mostly in a mixed noradrenergic/adrenergic pattern. Nine carriers (8.3%) had pituitary adenomas, presenting with acromegaly and/or prolactinoma symptoms: 3 growth hormone-secreting tumors, 4 prolactinomas and 1 mixed adenoma. Eleven (10.1%) had other neuroendocrine tumors, including primary hyperparathyroidism in 4 (1 with multifocal parathyroid adenomas), neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma/ganglioneuroma, C-cell hyperplasia and pancreatic NET. Seven (6.4%) had non-neuroendocrine tumors such as renal oncocytoma and renal cell carcinoma, and 3 carriers were asymptomatic. Maggacis et al. (2026) summarized the same series of 109 patients from 87 families.
